subject: english-language
topicDisplay: Component 2: 19th & 21st Century Non-Fiction Reading and Transactional/Persuasive Writing
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which is a form of non-fiction text?
questions.explain: Non-fiction includes articles, letters, speeches, reviews and diaries.

questions.q: A fact differs from an opinion because a fact:
questions.explain: Facts are verifiable; opinions express beliefs or judgements.

questions.q: To compare two non-fiction texts you should:
options: Examine similarities and differences in viewpoint and methods
questions.explain: Comparison focuses on perspectives, purposes and techniques across texts.

options: A question asked for effect, not for an answer
questions.explain: Rhetorical questions engage readers and imply an answer.

options: Grouping three words or phrases for emphasis
questions.explain: Triples create rhythm and emphasis in persuasive writing.

options: Writing only in the past tense
questions.explain: Direct address involves the reader and makes writing more persuasive.

options: Provoke an emotional response in the reader
questions.explain: Emotive words appeal to feelings to persuade.

options: The level of formality suited to audience and purpose
questions.explain: Register should match the audience, purpose and form (e.g. a formal letter).

questions.q: Writing a formal letter to a council to persuade them to build a park should use:
options: A formal register with clear structure and persuasive devices
questions.explain: Transactional writing must suit form, audience and purpose.
Synthesis draws together relevant points from multiple sources.

options: A short personal story used to engage the reader
questions.explain: Anecdotes make persuasive writing relatable and engaging.

questions.q: Identifying a writer's 'purpose' means working out whether they aim to:
options: Inform, persuade, argue, advise or entertain
questions.explain: Purpose shapes tone, structure and techniques.

options: Acknowledges an opposing view before rebutting it
questions.explain: Addressing counter-arguments strengthens a persuasive case.

questions.q: A 19th-century travel account and a 21st-century blog on the same place are compared. A good response focuses on:
options: How each writer conveys attitudes and uses language for their audience
The paper they are printed on
questions.explain: Comparison examines viewpoint, tone and method across time.

questions.q: Statistics are used in persuasive writing to:
options: Add credibility and support a point
questions.explain: Facts and figures lend authority to an argument.

questions.q: 'Tone' in a non-fiction text refers to:
options: The writer's attitude conveyed through language
questions.explain: Tone (e.g. serious, humorous, angry) is created through word choice and style.

questions.q: An effective persuasive opening might use:
options: A hook such as a striking fact, question or anecdote
questions.explain: A strong opening engages the reader and signals the argument.

questions.q: To write a speech encouraging students to recycle, effective techniques include:
options: Direct address, rule of three and emotive language
questions.explain: A range of rhetorical devices suits a persuasive speech.
